what: A choice explanation says a loop compiles and only changes a copy. In fact that loop does not compile.
evidence: Option "for i, n := range nums { n = nums[i] * 2 }" has the why-text "Still writes into the copy n. Reading nums[i] isn't enough...". When I ran that loop on Go 1.27.3 in a scratch module, it failed with: ./main.go:7:9: declared and not used: n (n is assigned but never read).
fix: Change the why-text to: "It doesn't even compile: n is only written, never read, so Go says declared and not used: n. And the left side of = must be nums[i]." Or swap in a distractor that compiles, e.g. for i, n := range nums { n = n * 2; _ = i }.

what: The page credits the cap-4 starter array to a Go 1.26 change, but Go 1.25.1 already gives cap 4 for this exact program, so the 1.24.7 vs 1.27.3 difference can't be pinned on 1.26.
evidence: Panel 19: "since Go 1.26 the compiler can give a loop's first append a small starter shelf". Notebook: "since Go 1.26, the first append in a loop can use a small starter array on the stack, which is the cap 4 you saw in panel 19". go.dev/blog/allocation-optimizations (fetched) does describe the append-site starter under 'Upgrade to Go 1.26!'. But running grow.go in a scratch module (go 1.24 go.mod, GOTOOLCHAIN=local) gives: go1.24.7 'len 1 cap 1 / len 2 cap 2 / len 3 cap 4'; go1.25.1 (/usr/local/go1.25.1) 'len 1 cap 4 / len 2 cap 4 / len 3 cap 4'; go1.27.3 the same as 1.25.1. Related: go/ch28 panel 9 says "That's new in Go 1.26 ... In chapter 9 it started at 1!", which contradicts ch9, where Go 1.27.3 starts at 4 and only 1.24.7 starts at 1 (see the separate go/ch28 finding).
fix: Say 'newer Go versions (1.25 and later on this machine) give the first append a small starter array on the stack; the Go blog describes the 1.26 version of this'. Or keep only what the run proves: '1.24.7 grew 1, 2, 4; 1.27.3 started at 4'.

what: The notebook says nil-map panics show 'runtime error', but a nil-map write panics without those words.
evidence: "'runtime error' means a check built into Go fired: an index out of range, a division of integers by zero, and later nil maps and nil pointers." A scratch run on Go 1.27.3 of `var m map[string]int; m["a"] = 1` prints "panic: assignment to entry in nil map", with no 'runtime error:' (the Go plan for ch12 quotes the same text). Nil pointers do say 'runtime error: invalid memory address...'.
fix: "... an index out of range, integer division by zero, and later nil pointers. (Writing to a nil map panics too, with its own wording.)"

what: The page states as fact a rule that Go libraries don't actually follow every time.
evidence: "Every Go library follows one rule: bad input gets a receipt, never a panic." The standard library panics on bad input in documented places, e.g. regexp.MustCompile, template.Must and strings.Repeat with a negative count. The recap repeats it: "Bad input gets an error value, never a panic."
fix: "Go's standard library almost always hands bad input a receipt, not a panic. Your code should too." (The recap can keep the advice form, which is fine as advice.)

what: The Delve command sequence is unverified, and it is probably one step short of reaching pick.
evidence: Lab: "(dlv) step   go INTO the call on this line: you're now inside label (s)", "(dlv) args", "(dlv) step   into pick", "(dlv) print n   n is 5". Delve usually stops on the callee's func line after a step-in, so from label's first stop it takes two steps to get inside pick. Then the first `next` lands on line 6, not on the panic. The page says the card isn't a captured run. I couldn't check it: installing dlv into the scratch folder was denied.
fix: Have someone with Delve run the session once and adjust the card. Or add 'step again if you're not yet on the return line' after each step.
